headline: Houthi strikes kill 12 at Riyadh airport in the worst attack on Saudi Arabia in a decade, while the ASX closed up 0.64% and Pilbara Minerals had a rough day — down 5.4%.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS took a significant hit today, dropping 5.4% to close at $3.50. There was no specific news catalyst in today's data, but Pilbara continues to face headwinds from subdued lithium prices globally — the market for battery materials remains oversupplied and demand growth from EV makers hasn't been enough to lift prices. This is a structural drag on the whole lithium sector, not a Pilbara-specific problem.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft had a strong night last session, jumping 2.4% to $535. The market is rewarding its AI momentum — Azure cloud revenue grew 43% last quarter, and traders see Microsoft as one of the clearest beneficiaries of enterprise AI spending. It's now trading at what some analysts consider a discount to its own five-year average valuation, which is drawing buyers in.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two rose 1.9% last session to $213.44. GTA 6 buzz is helping — Nintendo confirmed the Switch 2 is technically capable of running GTA 6, though a port is ultimately Rockstar's call. Any GTA 6 platform expansion would be a big revenue tailwind for Take-Two, which owns Rockstar. Markets are taking it as a positive signal.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google's parent Alphabet gained 0.87% last session to $347.86. The good news is real: Google Cloud revenue surged 82% to $24.8 billion last quarter, and the Gemini AI app hit 950 million monthly users. Cloud is increasingly becoming a bigger growth engine than traditional Search, which the market likes. Free cash flow pressure is a watch point, but the growth story remains compelling.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE slipped 1.43% today to $93.52. Emerging market funds like this one are sensitive to global risk appetite and the US dollar — when tensions rise (like the Middle East escalation today with Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia), investors tend to pull back from riskier emerging market exposure. Nothing structurally wrong here.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI dipped 1.02% today to $17.39. This ASX-listed AI ETF tracks global AI-focused companies and can be a bit volatile day-to-day. No specific news catalyst — likely some profit-taking after recent strength in the AI theme. The long-term AI tailwind remains firmly intact.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS edged down 0.41% to $545.68 in today's ASX session. This ETF mirrors the US total share market and its ASX-listed price can lag the actual US market move — last night the S&P 500 and NASDAQ both gained, so today's minor dip here is likely a pricing quirk or currency effect rather than any real weakness.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG nudged up 0.14% to $76.13 today — a quiet, steady session. This broadly diversified fund does its job smoothing out the noise. Nothing to see here, in the best possible way.

watch_today.title: Pilbara Minerals — biggest mover today, down 5.4%
watch_today.detail: PLS closed at $3.50, now down 48% on your total investment. This is painful but it's a structural lithium sector story, not a Pilbara-specific collapse. The long-term thesis — that lithium demand from EVs will recover — is intact, but the timeline has stretched. Unless you fundamentally no longer believe in the lithium cycle, this is a hold. Selling now locks in a big loss at the bottom of the cycle.

watch_today.title: Microsoft — strong night, up 2.4%
watch_today.detail: MSFT hit $535 last night on the back of 43% Azure cloud growth and strong AI momentum. You're up 20.75% overall on this position. The long-term AI story here is as strong as ever — Azure is growing faster than rivals and Microsoft's enterprise AI products are getting real traction. No reason to do anything but sit on this one.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — down 1% today, still in the red overall
watch_today.detail: The Global X AI ETF slipped another 1% today and sits 7.9% below your buy-in. The AI theme is still one of the strongest structural trends in markets — Google's Gemini hitting 950M users and Microsoft's Azure surging 43% are the real-world proof. Short-term dips like this in a thematic ETF are normal. Hold and let the theme play out.

watch_today.title: Take-Two — up 1.9% last night, GTA 6 buzz building
watch_today.detail: TTWO rose to $213.44 last night. Nintendo confirmed the Switch 2 can technically run GTA 6, and a port is Rockstar's call. Any platform expansion for GTA 6 would be a meaningful revenue boost for Take-Two. You're still down 8% overall on this position, but the GTA 6 release cycle is the long-term catalyst — hold and let it play out.

watch_today.title: Middle East tensions rising — watch oil prices
watch_today.detail: Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport killed 12 people overnight — the worst attack on the kingdom in a decade. Oil (WTI crude) ticked up slightly to $91.85 but hasn't spiked dramatically yet. If the conflict escalates further, oil could move sharply higher. That's inflationary, which is bad for bonds and can weigh on growth stocks. Worth watching this week.

watch_today.title: Gold hitting all-time highs — a signal worth noting
watch_today.detail: Gold surged 1.43% to $4,216/oz last night. When gold rallies this hard, it usually means investors are nervous — about geopolitics, inflation, or both. Right now it's likely a mix of Middle East escalation and macro uncertainty. Your portfolio has no direct gold exposure, but rising gold often precedes volatility in equities. Just something to be aware of.

world.summary: The Middle East is back in crisis mode, with Houthi rebels from Yemen escalating attacks on Saudi Arabia to their most deadly level in years. Elsewhere, Palestinian elections are delayed again and Iran is threatening wider shipping disruptions.

stories.title: Houthi strike on Riyadh airport kills 12 — worst attack on Saudi Arabia in a decade
stories.why_it_matters: Yemen's Houthi rebels launched a missile and drone strike on Riyadh's main international airport on Saturday, killing 12 people and injuring hundreds more. Reuters describes it as the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in a decade. The strike is part of an intensifying Houthi campaign targeting Saudi Arabia, which had largely reached a fragile ceasefire with the group but appears to have re-entered open conflict. For everyday people, this raises the risk of oil supply disruptions — Saudi Arabia is the world's largest oil exporter — and adds to broader Middle East instability. Oil prices edged up but haven't spiked dramatically yet.

stories.title: How a series of miscalculations restarted Saudi Arabia's war in Yemen
stories.why_it_matters: CNN has published an in-depth analysis of how the Saudi-Houthi conflict reignited after a period of relative calm. A series of diplomatic and military miscalculations on both sides apparently unravelled the ceasefire agreement that had held since 2023. The piece explains that neither side expected the other to escalate so quickly, and now both are locked into a cycle of retaliation. This is important context — this isn't a random flare-up but the product of months of behind-the-scenes tensions boiling over.

stories.title: Iran warns attacks on ships not limited to the Strait of Hormuz
stories.why_it_matters: Iran's Revolutionary Guard (the Pasdaran — Iran's elite military force) has warned that attacks on commercial shipping vessels will not be confined to the Strait of Hormuz, the critical chokepoint through which about 20% of global oil passes. This is a significant escalation in rhetoric. Broader shipping attacks would affect global supply chains and energy costs worldwide — including in Australia, which relies on imported fuel. Combined with the Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia, the entire Gulf region is becoming increasingly volatile.

stories.title: Palestinian elections postponed until September 2027
stories.why_it_matters: Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas (Abu Mazen) has postponed Palestinian elections until 11 September 2027. Palestinian elections have been repeatedly delayed for years — the last ones were held in 2006. The delay signals continued political paralysis within Palestinian leadership at a time when the region desperately needs legitimate governance structures. For the broader peace process, it's another setback.

politics.summary: Thin day for Australian domestic political news, with the main story being industry criticism of the RBA over interest rates. No major parliamentary or policy announcements today.

stories.title: Weld Australia slams RBA over rising interest rates
stories.why_it_matters: Industry group Weld Australia has publicly criticised the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) over its ongoing interest rate increases, arguing the rate rises are damaging local manufacturing and small businesses. When the RBA lifts rates, borrowing costs go up for businesses, making it harder to invest and hire. Weld Australia represents companies in the welding and fabrication sector and says many of its members are being squeezed between higher loan repayments and softer demand. It's a reminder that while rate rises aim to slow inflation, they create real pain for industries that rely on credit to operate.

ai.summary: AI safety and regulation dominated the headlines this weekend, with major labs reportedly preparing for the possibility of losing control of their own systems, California's governor signing an AI oversight order, and the UK's human rights committee weighing in on regulation.

stories.title: Major AI companies preparing for the possibility of AI 'getting out of control'
stories.why_it_matters: Reports this weekend say leading AI companies — including the biggest labs — are quietly developing internal plans for scenarios where their AI systems behave in ways that can't be predicted or controlled. This is sometimes called 'loss of control' risk, and it's moving from a theoretical concern to something companies are actively war-gaming. It suggests the people building these systems are taking the risks more seriously than their public messaging sometimes implies. For everyday people, it's a signal that even the optimists inside these labs acknowledge the technology is entering genuinely new territory.

stories.title: California Governor signs AI oversight executive order with 'kill switch' provision
stories.why_it_matters: California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed an executive order increasing oversight of AI systems operating in the state, including a proposed 'kill switch' — a mechanism that would allow authorities to shut down AI systems that pose a risk to public safety. California is home to most of the world's biggest AI companies (Google, OpenAI, Meta, etc.), so its regulations effectively become de facto global rules. A kill switch provision is a significant step — it means the state is reserving the right to forcibly halt AI systems, not just fine companies after the fact.

stories.title: Trump calls for AI industry to police itself on safety — Silicon Valley cheers
stories.why_it_matters: President Trump has publicly called for the AI industry to regulate itself on safety rather than face government-imposed rules — a stark contrast to California's approach. AI founders and investors in Silicon Valley are reportedly enthusiastic, seeing self-regulation as far preferable to government mandates. Critics argue self-policing has a poor track record in tech (think social media). The divergence between federal and state approaches to AI regulation in the US is growing — which creates real uncertainty for companies operating nationally.

stories.title: UK Joint Committee on Human Rights calls for stronger AI rights protections
stories.why_it_matters: The UK Parliament's Joint Committee on Human Rights has released a report saying the UK's current approach to AI regulation is 'strong on rights but light on machinery' — meaning the principles are good but the enforcement mechanisms are weak. The committee is pushing for more concrete rules around AI's impact on privacy, discrimination, and free expression. The UK is trying to position itself as a pro-innovation but responsible AI hub post-Brexit, and this report highlights the tension between moving fast and protecting people's rights.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final is done — Roosters pipped the Knights 19-18 in one of the closest GFs in years. The AFL is deep into trade period with some big names on the move, and Carlton is dealing with an off-field health scare.

stories.title: Roosters defeat Knights 19-18 in nail-biting NRL Grand Final
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters claimed the 2026 NRL premiership with a one-point win over the Newcastle Knights — 19-18 — at Accor Stadium on Sunday 4 October. It doesn't get closer than that in a Grand Final. The Knights had a real shot at their first title in years but fell just short. A classic for the ages.

stories.title: AFL Trade Period: Blakey, Whitfield and more — the state of play on major deals
stories.why_it_matters: AFL trade period is in full swing with some big names in play. Hawthorn's Dylan Moore look-alike Jack Blakey and GWS Giants captain Stephen Whitfield are among the headline acts being linked with moves. AFL.com.au has a full breakdown of where negotiations stand. This is the time of year when clubs reshape their lists for a tilt at 2027 — the next few weeks of trade period will define several clubs' seasons before they've even started.

stories.title: Carlton releases statement after two Blues hospitalised
stories.why_it_matters: Carlton Football Club has released a statement after two Blues players were hospitalised, though the club has not disclosed the nature of the incident or the players involved. The club says both players are receiving appropriate care. This is an developing story — details are scant but it's clearly serious enough to warrant an official club response. Worth watching for updates.

stories.title: Fox Sports land NRL fan favourite as new analyst in stunning coup
stories.why_it_matters: Fox Sports has reportedly signed a popular NRL personality as a new analyst for their coverage — described by the Telegraph as a 'fan favourite'. The identity of the signing hasn't been confirmed in the article title, but Fox is clearly making moves to bolster its NRL commentary lineup in the off-season. For NRL fans, it's good news if it freshens up the broadcast.

markets.summary: A solid day across the board. The ASX 200 closed up 0.64%, US markets (last night's session) were also in the green — S&P 500 up 0.59%, NASDAQ up 0.64%. Gold surged to $4,216 — a big move driven by Middle East tensions and general investor nervousness. The Aussie dollar inched up to nearly 70 US cents.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Solid session today — broad-based gains across most sectors.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session: modest gains as tech and AI names led the way.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Last night's session: NASDAQ matched the broader market — Microsoft and Google both helped.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Big move — gold is surging as investors seek safe havens amid Middle East escalation.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil nudged higher despite the Houthi strike on Riyadh — markets may be waiting to see if the conflict widens before pricing in a bigger risk premium.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar crept up toward 70 US cents — stronger commodity prices and a positive risk tone helped.
